Whooping crane chicks emerge from eggs incubated at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C] after a developmental period of 29 days [ab = 29 days], a duration that aligns closely with the incubation requirements of other large Gruidae species. These precocial chicks are surprisingly heavy at hatching, with a wet weight at birth of 137.2 grams [Wwb = 137.2 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk reserves that support their early development. This initial body mass is considerable when compared to the hatchling masses of smaller cranes like the Demoiselle crane, and it provides a robust foundation for the rapid growth phase that follows. Field studies have shown that the body temperature of the incubating adult maintains a remarkably stable incubation environment at 36.2 °C, which is critical for proper embryogenesis. The chicks are brooded intensively during their first weeks, and their development proceeds under a strict thermal regime that influences their growth trajectory.

During the active metabolic period when core body temperatures average 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], Whooping crane chicks reach a critical developmental milestone: fledging occurs at 78 days since birth [tx = 78 days since birth]. This achievement, marking the ability to achieve sustained flight, is a pivotal transition in the life of a young crane. The fledgling then undergoes a period of continued learning and foraging practice under parental guidance. This developmental schedule is a direct consequence of the rapid skeletal and feather development supported by the chick's high metabolic rate at 40.4 °C. Following fledging, the immature birds gradually increase their independence, though they typically remain with their parents throughout their first winter. This prolonged post-fledging association is crucial for learning the complex migratory routes and foraging techniques necessary for survival in the wild.

This relatively late puberty is characteristic of long-lived, slowly maturing bird species. The attainment of gonadal maturation at 234 days since birth [tp = 234 days since birth] does not, however, immediately translate into successful breeding; young adults often wait several more years before establishing a territory and forming a pair bond at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. Comparative data from related species suggest that this delayed sexual maturation is linked to the energetically demanding courtship displays and the extensive parental care required to raise a single chick successfully. The thermal environment at 40.4 °C is maintained throughout this maturation period and supports the high metabolic costs associated with song production and dance displays.

First brood attempts in Whooping cranes occur notably later than the onset of puberty, with the time since birth at first brood recorded as 1040 days [tR = 1040 days] under conditions where core body temperature averages 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This extended interval between achieving sexual maturity and initiating reproduction reflects the considerable social and ecological challenges faced by young cranes. This major life-history investment sees Whooping cranes typically laying a clutch of one to two eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of one to two eggs], and they usually produce approximately two clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately two clutches per year]. The maximum annual reproductive rate is therefore constrained to about 2 offspring per 365 days, a value among the lowest recorded for any North American bird, and occurs when adults are functioning at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C].

The maximum lifespan of the Whooping crane in the wild is estimated at 24 years [am = 24 years], a figure derived from long-term banding studies of wild populations where core body temperatures average 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This impressive longevity is a reflection of their slow life-history pace, which includes delayed reproduction and extended parental care. The ultimate wet weight for a healthy adult Whooping crane is approximately 6948.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 6948.5 grams], although males, being the larger sex, can reach an ultimate wet weight of as much as 7300 grams [Wwi = 7300 grams] under optimal foraging conditions. These body masses place the Whooping crane among the world's tallest flying birds, with a wingspan exceeding two meters. The sustained high body temperature of 40.4 °C throughout adult life drives the metabolic machinery needed to maintain such a large body mass and to support the energetic demands of long-distance migration between their breeding grounds in Wood Buffalo National Park and wintering areas along the Texas Gulf Coast.
